title: Referred for carpal tunnel, with weakness that is climbing
objective: Interpreting abnormal findings: axonal versus demyelinating, focal versus diffuse, acute versus chronic
secondaryObjectives: Recognize demyelinating patterns on nerve conduction studies: prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocity, temporal dispersion and conduction block, with prolonged F-wave and H-reflex latencies

brief.situation: 11:00 in an outpatient electrodiagnostic lab. You are the physical therapist performing the study. Ms. Park, 38, is referred by her primary care physician: 'Numbness in both hands, probable carpal tunnel syndrome. EMG and nerve conduction studies, please.'
handover: The intake form says the numbness began 'about a week ago'. She walked in slowly with her partner.
Equipment: the nerve conduction and EMG system, a pulse oximeter and a blood pressure cuff.
Clinic policy: a patient who may be getting weaker or short of breath goes to the emergency department by ambulance; tell the referring physician.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question, test and study takes the time on its button. Decide what to study, what the findings mean and what to do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Is this carpal tunnel syndrome? What do the studies show, and what do you do?

parts.label: Interpretation
parts.criteria: Not focal: prolonged distal latencies, slowed velocities, conduction block, dispersion and absent or prolonged F-waves in all four nerves with preserved amplitudes are diffuse, demyelinating and acute (6 days, ascending, after diarrhea): suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome; an early normal study would not exclude it.
parts.modelAnswer: This is not carpal tunnel syndrome. The changes are in all four nerves, not just the median at the wrist: prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction, conduction block and dispersion, and absent or prolonged F-waves, with amplitudes preserved. That is a diffuse, acute demyelinating pattern. With six days of ascending tingling and weakness after diarrhea and no reflexes, I suspect Guillain-Barre syndrome.

parts.label: Action
parts.criteria: Checks breathing (single breath count under 20, breathless lying flat); stops the study rather than adding a long needle EMG; 911 to the emergency department; tells the referring physician.
parts.modelAnswer: She cannot count to 20 in one breath and is breathless lying flat, so her breathing is at risk. I stop the study, call 911 for the emergency department and call her physician.

scoring.modelReasoning: Interpret a study by distribution, pathology and time course. Here every nerve tested shows prolonged distal latencies, slowed velocities, conduction block, dispersion and absent or prolonged F-waves with preserved amplitudes: diffuse (not the focal median slowing of carpal tunnel syndrome), demyelinating (not axonal) and acute. With six days of ascending tingling and weakness after diarrhea and absent reflexes, that is suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome; electrodiagnosis supports an early diagnosis, though a normal early study would not exclude it. Breathing decides urgency: a single breath count under 20 and breathlessness lying flat mean 911 to the emergency department now, without adding a long needle study, and a call to the referring physician.
